# Ionothermal Synthesis of Metal-Organic Frameworks Using Low-Melting Metal Salt Precursors

**Authors:** Tyler J. Azbell; Tristan A. Pitt; Melissa M. Bollmeyer; Christina Cong; Kyle M. Lancaster; Phillip J. Milner

**Affiliations:** [a]Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14850, United States

## Abstract

Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are porous, crystalline materials constructed from organic linkers and inorganic nodes with myriad potential applications in chemical separations, catalysis, and drug delivery. A major barrier to the application of MOFs is their poor scalability, as most frameworks are prepared under highly dilute solvothermal conditions using toxic organic solvents. Herein, we demonstrate that combining a range of linkers with low-melting metal halide (hydrate) salts leads directly to high-quality MOFs without added solvent. Frameworks prepared these under ionothermal conditions possess porosities comparable to those prepared under traditional solvothermal conditions. In addition, we report the ionothermal syntheses of two frameworks that cannot be prepared directly under solvothermal conditions. Overall, the user-friendly method reported herein should be broadly applicable to the discovery and synthesis of stable metal-organic materials.

## Abstract

Using low-melting metal (hydrate) salts as both the precursor and the solvent for ionothermal synthesis, a range of stable metal-organic frameworks can be prepared with high crystallinity and porosity and minimal use of organic solvents.

## Introduction

Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are porous, crystalline coordination polymers constructed from organic linkers and inorganic nodes that are promising next-generation materials for a range of applications, including chemical separations, gas storage, drug delivery, and heterogeneous catalysis.[1–4] Among MOFs, those constructed from basic linkers, including salicylates, pyrazolates, and triazolates, stand out due to their excellent chemical stabilities and highly modular structures.[5–9] However, the chemical stability of these MOFs is a double-edged sword, as poorly reversible metal-ligand bond formation generally necessitates harsh solvothermal reaction conditions to achieve high crystallinities. In particular, pyrazolate and triazolate MOFs are typically prepared under highly dilute reaction conditions (<0.01 M) in organic solvents such as N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) due to the poor solubility of the corresponding organic linkers.[10,11] Techno-economic analyses confirm that organic solvents make up a large portion of the cost of MOFs on scale.[12] Therefore, scalable methods for the synthesis of MOFs prepared from basic linkers with minimal solvent use would greatly accelerate their translation to industry.

Synthesis methods without added solvent are cost-effective and green alternatives to traditional, solvothermal (ST) methods.[13] Such MOF syntheses are generally carried out under mechanochemical conditions, in which solids are ground together with or without added liquid. Mechanochemical methods are a reliable means of preparing some carboxylate- and salicylate-based frameworks in comparable quality to solvothermal methods.[13–19] However, examples of mechanochemical and solvent-free preparations of azolate-based MOFs materials remain largely limited to simple zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIFs).[20,21] Likewise, mechanochemical methods rely on specialized equipment such as ball mills or extruders, hindering their broad applicability for non-experts. Ionothermal (IT) syntheses, in which an ionic liquid or molten metal salt is used as a solvent and/or structure directing agent are another promising alternative to solvothermal methods using organic solvents.[22] Historically, ionothermal syntheses have been utilized to access ZIFs and carboxylate MOFs with an emphasis on crystallization kinetic control and the induction of chirality via the inclusion of ionic liquids within the framework.[17,23–31] Nonetheless, a MOF synthesis in which a low-melting metal salt behaves as both the reaction solvent and metal precursor would minimize the waste associated with MOF preparation. However, it remains unclear if such an ionothermal strategy can be generalized beyond simple materials such as ZIFs and carboxylate MOFs.[17,27–31] As such, ionothermal methods have significant untapped potential for the benchtop-scalable, user-friendly, and time-efficient synthesis of stable MOFs with minimal solvent use.

Herein, we demonstrate that simply heating low-melting metal salt (hydrates) and organic linkers together above the melting point of the metal salt is a general method for the direct synthesis of stable azolate and salicylate MOFs, especially those constructed from late first-row transition metals (Fe, Co, Ni, Zn). The frameworks prepared in this manner possess crystallinities and 77 K N2 Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface areas comparable to materials prepared under conventional, highly dilute solvothermal conditions. In addition, we demonstrate the first ionothermal synthesis of M(III) members of the MOF-74 family, which cannot be prepared directly under solvothermal conditions. Overall, our work demonstrates that the ionothermal synthesis of MOFs using low-melting metal salt hydrates as both the metal precursor and reaction medium represents a simple and broadly applicable method for the synthesis of both known and new metal-organic materials.

## Results and Discussion

The proposed ionothermal synthesis of MOFs uniquely requires low-melting metal salts that can serve as both the MOF precursor and reaction medium. However, the high temperatures required to melt most anhydrous metal salts (e.g., CoCl2, melting point = 735 °C) precludes their use as ionic liquids for MOF synthesis.[32] Intriguingly, metal salt hydrates (e.g. CoCl2∙6H2O, melting point = 86 °C) typically have much lower melting points (Supporting Information or SI Table S22) than anhydrous metal salts and organic linkers (SI Figure S144), yet these precursors have not been previously studied as solvents for the ionothermal synthesis of porous materials.[32–36]

Herein, ionothermal MOF syntheses are performed using judiciously chosen low-melting metal (hydrate) salts in Teflon autoclaves (see SI for details). After confirming via powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) that crystalline MOFs are present in the crude ionothermal reaction mixtures, solvent washes were performed to remove soluble impurities, as is standard practice for MOF synthesis.[37] Solvent volumes were minimized by employing Soxhlet extraction, and DMF was avoided when feasible. All samples were activated under dynamic vacuum and stored in a N2-filled glovebox prior to characterization. In all cases, the quality of prepared frameworks was assessed by PXRD, SEM, infrared (IR) spectroscopy, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and 77 K N2 surface area analysis. The elemental purity of all samples was further validated qualitatively by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and quantitatively by combustion analysis. All frameworks were prepared under ionothermal conditions at least twice to demonstrate reproducibility and under reported solvothermal conditions for direct comparison.

The M2Cl2(btdd) (M = V, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu; btdd2− = bis(1,2,3-triazolo[4,5-b],[4′,5′-i])dibenzo[1,4]dioxin) family of MOFs, which bear coordinatively unsaturated metal centers, embody the synthetic challenges associated with preparing azolate MOFs (Figure 1a–b).[7,10,38,39] Due to the poor solubility of H2btdd, these MOFs are generally prepared under highly dilute (0.001–0.005 M) solvothermal conditions in DMF and thus are routinely made on small scale in the laboratory. Improved methods for preparing Ni2Cl2(btdd) have been reported, but these syntheses still require dilute reactions conditions[38] and/or complex instrumentation.[40]

We began by investigating the ionothermal synthesis of Co2Cl2(btdd), also known as MAF-X27l-Cl (MAF = metal azolate framework),[41] as a representative member of this family of materials. Simply heating stoichiometric amounts of CoCl2∙6H2O and H2btdd together in a Teflon autoclave at 160 °C yielded Co2Cl2(btdd) (referred to herein as Co2Cl2(btdd)-IT) in good yield (66% on average), as confirmed by PXRD (Figure 1c, see SI Section 3 for details). Importantly, analysis of a crude ionothermal reaction mixture (i.e., before washing with organic solvent to remove soluble impurities) by PXRD (SI Figures S12, S139, S142) revealed that Co2Cl2(btdd) is indeed the major crystalline product of the reaction. In addition, SEM confirmed the presence of well-defined hexagonal 5 μm rod-shaped crystals with additional smaller (<200 nm) crystallites, consistent with the reported morphology of M2Cl2(btdd) MOFs,[42] in both the crude reaction mixture (SI Figure S22) and after washing to remove soluble impurities (Figure 1d, SI Figure S22). This finding supports that the MOF does not form or recrystallize during the solvent washes used to remove insoluble impurities. The crystallinity of the obtained MOF was comparable to that of material prepared under traditional solvothermal conditions at a linker concentration of ~0.002 M (Co2Cl2(btdd)-ST) (SI Figure S12). Soaking the MOF in DMF and methanol (MeOH) (“Standard”) or by eliminating the use of DMF by soaking in DMSO followed by Soxhlet extraction with MeOH (“Soxhlet”) led to comparable 77 K N2 Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface areas (Standard: 2322 ± 2 m2/g; Soxhlet: 2305 ± 10 m2/g; SI Figure S14). These values are comparable to the BET surface area of MOF prepared under solvothermal conditions (2438 ± 14 m2/g, SI Figure S10) and higher than that previously reported for this material (1912 m2/g) (Table 1).[42] Finally, combustion elemental analysis was also consistent with the predicted elemental composition for Co2Cl2(btdd) (SI Table S2), confirming a lack of significant graphitization under these conditions.[47] Utilizing the Soxhlet extraction procedure enables Co2Cl2(btdd) to be prepared using less than 0.8 L solvent per g of linker without the need for DMF, as opposed to 8 L of solvent per g of linker (4 L of DMF) required for the traditional solvothermal synthesis. Overall, these data confirm the high quality of Co2Cl2(btdd)-IT compared to material prepared under solvothermal conditions.

Several control experiments were carried out to probe the pathway for Co2Cl2(btdd) formation under ionothermal conditions (see SI Section 14 for details). As mentioned above, PXRD (SI Figures S12, S139, S142) and SEM (SI Figure S22) reproducibly confirmed that Co2Cl2(btdd) is the major crystalline species present in the crude ionothermal reaction mixture. Thus, the role of the DMF and MeOH washes is simply to remove soluble impurities and not to aid in MOF formation.[37] Additionally, an attempted ionothermal synthesis using anhydrous CoCl2 at 160 °C yielded unreacted starting materials (SI Figure S139), confirming the need for waters of hydration to reduce the melting point of the metal salt precursor. We cannot rule out that water also serves a dual role as a supercritical solvent under these conditions. Heating H2btdd and CoCl2∙6H2O together at 90 °C—only 3 °C above the melting point of the metal salt—yielded an amorphous solid (SI Figure S141). These findings indicate that simply melting CoCl2∙6H2O and H2btdd together well above the melting point of the metal salt produces Co2Cl2(btdd) without added solvent.

To evaluate the scope of triazolate MOFs that can be prepared under ionothermal conditions, we extended our investigation to the isostructural Ni-analogue Ni2Cl2(btdd) (Ni2Cl2(btdd)-IT, Figure 1a–b), also known as MAF-X28l-Cl,[41] and the polymorphic Zn-analogue Zn5Cl4(btdd)3 (Zn5Cl4(btdd)3-IT, Figure 2a–b), also known as MFU-4l.[43,48] As with Co2Cl2(btdd)-IT, Ni2Cl2(btdd)-IT can be prepared directly from NiCl2∙6H2O (melting point = 140 °C) and H2btdd at 160 °C without added solvent (see SI Section 4 for details). The high crystallinity of Ni2Cl2(btdd)-IT before and after washing to remove soluble impurities was confirmed by PXRD and SEM (Figure 1c–d; SI Figures S26 and S37). Critically, Ni2Cl2(btdd)-IT possesses a 77 K N2 BET surface area of 2438 ± 82 m2/g (SI Figure S28), comparable to the Co analogue but significantly higher than that measured for Ni2Cl2(btdd) prepared under solvothermal conditions (1973 ± 19 m2/g) (Table 1).[38] This represents one of the highest surface area reported to date for Ni2Cl2(btdd), a promising MOF for water harvesting and corrosive gas capture.[10,38] Attempts to utilize Soxhlet extraction to wash this (and all other Ni(II)-based MOFs prepared herein) with DMF or DMSO resulted in significant loss of crystallinity and porosity. Therefore, MeOH Soxhlet extraction was employed after the DMF soaks, resulting in a sample of Ni2Cl2(btdd) with a BET surface area comparable to the solvothermally synthesized analogue (2028 ± 17 m2/g) (SI Figure S28).

Given the high melting point of ZnCl2 (290 °C), initial attempts to prepare Zn5Cl4(btdd)3 directly from ZnCl2 and H2btdd resulted in partially degraded or graphitized material.[47] In order to access high-quality samples of this framework, a 6:1:1 eutectic mixture of ZnCl2, NaCl, and KCl with a melting point of 225 °C was employed as the reaction medium under anhydrous conditions instead.[49] The excess NaCl and KCl could be washed away by soaking the synthesized MOF in water. Ionothermal synthesis via this eutectic route afforded Zn5Cl4(btdd)3-IT with a PXRD pattern matching that of the solvothermal analogue Zn5Cl4(btdd)3-ST and the simulated pattern for this material (Figure 2d, see SI section 5 for details).[43] The SEM images of Zn5Cl4(btdd)3-IT also revealed some well-defined cubic crystals approximately 1–10 μm in length, in line with the expected morphology of this material, along with other less well-defined crystallites (Figure 2c, SI Figure S52).[43,50] In addition, 77 K N2 adsorption measurements demonstrate that Zn5Cl4(btdd)3-IT has a BET surface area of 2524 ± 10 m2/g (SI Figure S43), which agrees well with both the surface area of the solvothermal sample (2750 ± 4 m2/g) and values reported previously in the literature (2750 m2/g) (Table 1).[43] The sample purified via Soxhlet extraction with MeOH possessed a similar BET surface area (2317 ± 10 m2/g). While the obtained MOF was slightly gray in color, indicative of partial graphitization,[47] the carbon weight % of Zn5Cl4(btdd)3-IT measured by combustion analysis (34.21%) matches the theoretical value (34.27%), suggesting that the degree of graphitization is likely minimal (SI Table S6). Notably, because this synthesis was set up in a N2-filled glovebox to minimize hydrolysis of ZnCl2, we hypothesize that water is not necessary to form triazolate MOFs under solvent-free conditions, and that the molten salt itself directly facilitates MOF assembly in this case. Indeed, Zn5Cl4(btdd)3-IT was present before washing with any solvents (SI Figures S41, S52). Together, these results support that ionothermal methods can be generally employed to prepare Co, Ni, and Zn-based frameworks constructed from the btdd2− linker. Attempts to extend this ionothermal method to the synthesis of less robust Mn- and Cu-based analogues were unsuccessful,[10,51] suggesting that ionothermal methods are best suited for the synthesis of thermally and acid-stable azolate frameworks.

Encouraged by the successful synthesis of several triazolate frameworks under ionothermal conditions, we next investigated the generality of this strategy towards the synthesis of frameworks constructed from more basic pyrazolate linkers. One such framework of interest is Ni3(btp)2 (btp3− = 4,4’,4”-(benzene-1,3,5-triyl)tris(pyrazolate)), which is a thermally and chemically robust MOF bearing coordinatively unsaturated square planar Ni(II) centers that is capable of catalyzing the solvent-free cycloaddition of CO2 and epoxides to form cyclic carbonates (Figure 3, see SI Section 6 for details).[11,52] The traditional solvothermal synthesis of Ni3(btp)2 employs Ni(OAc)2∙4H2O as the metal precursor and is carried out in dilute DMF (0.05 M).[11] Switching from Ni(OAc)2∙4H2O, which decomposes upon heating, to NiCl2∙6H2O as the metal precursor and reaction medium enabled the ionothermal synthesis of Ni3(btp)2-IT under the same conditions employed to prepare Ni2Cl2(btdd)-IT (Figure 3). The crystallinity of Ni3(btp)2-IT was found to be superior to material prepared under the traditional solvothermal conditions by PXRD (Ni3(btp)2-ST, Figure 3d). Likewise, the BET surface area of Ni3(btp)2-IT (2602 ± 8 m2/g, SI Figure S58) is significantly higher than that of Ni3(btp)2-ST (2100 ± 11 m2/g) (Table 1).[11] This may be due in part to the presence of missing linker and/or node defects in Ni3(btp)2-IT, as evidenced by the presence of trace Cl in this sample by XPS even after soaking in DMF and methanol (SI Figure S61).[53] Similar to Ni2Cl2(btdd), attempts to reduce the solvent volumes required a modified washing procedure in which serial hot DMF washes were followed by a MeOH Soxhlet extraction. The resulting Ni3(btp)2-IT sample also demonstrated an increased surface area compared to the solvothermal material (2526 ± 3 m2/g, SI Figure S58). Together with the results obtained for the synthesis of Ni2Cl2(btdd)-IT, these findings suggest that ionothermal methods are promising alternatives to solvothermal methods for the synthesis of high surface area Ni-azolate MOFs.

These findings could be successfully extended to the synthesis of the flexible Ni-pyrazolate MOF Ni(bdp) (bdp2− = 1,4-benzene-4,4′-dipyrazolate) under ionothermal conditions (Figure 4, see SI section 7 for details).[44] An insoluble, porous orange solid (Ni(bdp)-IT) could be obtained by simply combining H2bdp and NiCl2∙6H2O at 160 °C. The PXRD of the resulting crystalline solid matched that previously reported for Ni(bdp)-ST prepared under solvothermal conditions (SI Figure S69).[44] SEM images revealed rhombic crystals surrounded by regions of shapeless crystals (Figure 4c) before washing, supporting the formation of this MOF via ionothermal synthesis. Consistently, the BET surface area of activated Ni(bdp)-IT obtained after simple Soxhlet extraction with acetonitrile (1124 ± 11 m2/g) is comparable to that previously reported for Ni(bdp) (1066 m2/g) (Table 1). This MOF could be prepared ionothermally using only 0.02 L acetonitrile per g linker, a significant improvement compared to the solvothermal synthesis, which requires 4.6 L of solvent per g linker.

Given the generality of this ionothermal strategy for the synthesis of MOFs constructed from basic pyrazolate and triazolate linkers, we aimed to expand our findings to MOFs constructed from another class of basic linkers: salicylates. Among salicylate MOFs, M2(dobdc) (dobdc4− = 2,5-dioxido-1,4-benzenedicarboxylate), also known as MOF-74 or CPO-27, and M2(m-dobdc) (m-dobdc4− = 4,6-dioxido-1,3-benzenedicarboxylate), stand out due to their high density of coordinatively unsaturated M(II) sites (Figures 4a–b).[46,54] Of primary interest are Co2(dobdc), which is a promising material for separating xylene isomers,[55] and Ni2(m-dobdc) (m-dobdc4− = 4,6-dioxido-1,3-benzenedicarboxylate), a record-holding material for H2 storage that was recently demonstrated to be one of the most chemically stable salicylate MOFs as well (Figure 5).[5,56] These and related frameworks are typically synthesized under dilute solvothermal conditions (0.01–0.05 M) using DMF, alcohols, or water as the solvent.[46,54,57–59] As such, ionothermal methods represent a promising alternative to synthesize salicylate MOFs constructed from late transition metals under solvent-free conditions. Therefore, we investigated whether the ionothermal conditions employed to prepare Co2Cl2(btdd) and Ni2Cl2(btdd) were generalizable to the synthesis of Co2(dobdc) and Ni2(m-dobdc) (see SI Sections 8 and 10 for details).

Initial attempts to synthesize Co2(dobdc) and Ni2(m-dobdc) directly from CoCl2∙6H2O and NiCl2∙6H2O, respectively, under ionothermal conditions at 160 °C were unsuccessful (not shown). However, simply increasing the reaction temperature to 200 °C was sufficient to enable the synthesis of phase-pure Co2(dobdc)-IT and Ni2(m-dobdc)-IT, as confirmed by PXRD (Figure 5c). The crystallinity of Co2(dobdc)-IT was comparable to that of material prepared under solvothermal conditions, while the crystallinity of Ni2(m-dobdc)-IT was more modest. These findings were confirmed by SEM: Co2(dobdc)-IT is composed of well-defined crystallites, including some hexagonal rods >10 μm in length (Figure 5d, SI Figure S91).[55] On the other hand, Ni2(m-dobdc)-IT consists of fuzzy microcrystalline particles (Figure 5d, SI Figure S118). Remarkably, well-defined single crystals of Co2(dobdc) were found to be present even in the crude ionothermal reaction mixture (SI Figure S91). As with the azolate MOFs discussed above, the 77 K N2 BET surface areas of Co2(dobdc)-IT and Ni2(m-dobdc)-IT are comparable to those of reference materials prepared under solvothermal conditions and to values reported in the literature (Table 1), reflecting their high quality.[45,46] Consistently, neither material was found to contain significant amounts of residual Cl, as confirmed by XPS (SI Figures S87, S114). As with Co2Cl2(btdd)-IT, the amount of solvent required to remove soluble impurities from Co2(dobdc)-IT could be minimized via Soxhlet extraction with only MeOH, resulting in a sample of Co2(dobdc)-IT with comparable surface area as material prepared using the standard washing procedure (1016 ± 1 m2/g, SI Figure S84). Intriguingly, Soxhlet extraction with MeOH was sufficient to purify Ni2(m-dobdc)-IT to produce high surface area material as well (1366 ± 2 m2/g, SI Figure S111). Therefore, ionothermal synthesis allows for DMF to be completely bypassed during the synthesis of these two MOFs.

Attempts to synthesize analogous frameworks that are less stable to acids, such as Mg2(dobdc), under ionothermal conditions resulted in amorphous materials. We ascribe this to the generation of HCl in situ, as linker deprotonation must be concurrent with chloride loss from the metal chloride salt. The generation of HCl is also a reasonable justification for the attenuated yields observed via this melt process as opposed to the mechanochemical synthesis of MOFs in the same family.[15,16,19] Since generated HCl is trapped in the sealed autoclave, an equilibrium between the melt and the gaseous HCl must be present; in other words, HCl likely modulates MOF formation, accounting for the excellent crystallinity of ionothermally synthesized MOFs. Nonetheless, these promising results suggest that ionothermal methods may be a general alternative to solvothermal methods for the synthesis of acid-stable Co- and Ni-based MOFs constructed from basic linkers.

Having demonstrated the generality of ionothermal methods for the synthesis of azolate and salicylate MOFs, we hypothesized that the unusual kinetic regime offered by ionothermal methods might enable the synthesis of new frameworks that cannot be synthesized directly under solvothermal conditions. To investigate this possibility, we targeted the synthesis of M(III) variants of the M2(dobdc) and M2(m-dobdc) families of materials. Although both frameworks can be prepared with a range of M(II) cations (e.g., Mg, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Cd),[45,54,60] the direct synthesis of M(III) variants of these frameworks remains unreported. Consistently, attempted direct syntheses of Fe2Cl2(dobdc) and Fe2Cl2(m-dobdc) from FeCl3∙6H2O and the corresponding linkers under the solvothermal conditions typically used to prepare Fe2(dobdc) and Fe2(m-dobdc) produced only amorphous solids (SI Figures S105 and S133). Previously reported Fe(III) variants of MOF-74 have been prepared via post-synthetic oxidation of highly air-sensitive Fe2(dobdc) with limited success.[61–65] Therefore, we investigated whether these understudied Fe(III) frameworks can be prepared directly under ionothermal conditions instead (see Sections 9 and 11 of the SI for details).

Initial attempts to prepare Fe(III) salicylate MOFs from FeCl3∙6H2O and H4dobdc or H4m-dobdc under ionothermal conditions at 160–180 °C were unsuccessful. Increasing the reaction temperature to 200 °C—the same temperature employed to prepare Co2(dobdc)-IT and Ni2(m-dobdc)-IT—produced crystalline solids with PXRD patterns similar to those of independently prepared samples of Fe2(dobdc) and Fe2(m-dobdc), respectively (Figure 6c), even before soaking to remove soluble impurities (SI Figures S92 and S119). These frameworks would be expected to adopt similar topologies as the corresponding Fe(II) frameworks with additional charge-balancing anions in the pores to compensate for the increase in metal formal oxidation state (Figure 6b). The obtained air-stable solids were assigned as Fe2X2(dobdc) and Fe2X2(m-dobdc) (X = Cl, OH) due to uncertainty regarding the charge-balancing anions present in the framework pores (see discussion below).

Consistent with the PXRD data, SEM images of Fe2X2(dobdc) (X = Cl, OH) before and after washing revealed clusters of ellipsoidal crystallites that range in size from 5–20 μm in length, akin to the SEM images of many MOF-74 analogues,[54,66,67] along with less well-defined particles (Figure 6d, SI Figure S103). In contrast, the SEM images of Fe2X2(m-dobdc) (X = Cl, OH) revealed poorly defined particles (Figure 6d, SI Figure S130), in line with the reduced crystallinity of this material. Further supporting the assigned structures, the 77 K N2 BET surface areas of Fe2X2(dobdc) (X = Cl, OH) (645 ± 1 m2/g) and Fe2X2(m-dobdc) (X = Cl, OH) (809 ± 1 m2/g) (Table 1) after gentle washing with methanol and dichloromethane are lower than those reported for Fe2(dobdc) (1350 m2/g)[68] and Fe2(m-dobdc) (1360 m2/g),[46] respectively. This is expected, as the additional species within the pores of the Fe(III) MOFs should reduce their free pore volumes, and the increase in molar mass of the material should accompany a decrease in surface area as well (see SI for discussion). Notably, the %C determined by combustion analysis of Fe2X2(dobdc) (X = Cl, OH) (29.96%) is comparable to the theoretical value (25.51–28.28%), suggesting that minimal graphitization of this material occurred under the reaction conditions (SI Table S13).

We employed Mössbauer spectroscopy to further support the formal oxidation state assignments of the novel Fe(III) MOFs (Figure 7). The Mössbauer spectrum of Fe2X2(dobdc) (X = Cl, OH) contains a doublet corresponding to a single Fe species with an isomer shift of 0.51 mm/s and a quadrupole splitting of 0.90 mm/s, consistent with an S = 5/2 Fe(III) species (SI Table S14). Likewise, Fe2X2(m-dobdc) (X = Cl, OH) possesses a similar Mössbauer spectrum with an isomer shift of 0.50 mm/s and a quadrupole splitting of 0.88 mm/s, again consistent with an S = 5/2 Fe(III) center (SI Table S19). These values are comparable to those previously reported for Fe(III) MOF-74 prepared by post-synthetic oxidation.[62] The Mössbauer spectra of the Fe(III) MOFs contrast with that of a reference sample of Fe2(dobdc), which contains a doublet with an increased isomer shift of 1.26(6) mm/s and a quadrupole splitting of 2.58 mm/s (Figure 7, SI Table S21). These parameters are consistent with a S = 2 Fe(II) center and are similar to reported values for this framework, as well.[63,64] Overall, the PXRD, SEM, 77 K N2 BET surface areas, and Mössbauer spectra are consistent with the structural assignment of Fe2X2(dobdc) and Fe2X2(m- dobdc) (X = Cl, OH) as Fe(III) analogues of M2(dobdc) and M2(m-dobdc) MOFs, respectively.

After establishing the likely structures of the new Fe(III) frameworks, we investigated the nature of the charge-balancing anions—Cl, OH, or a mixture of both—present within the pores. Combustion analysis of both materials revealed that the Cl wt% was low for both materials assuming molecular formulae of Fe2Cl2(dobdc) (Table S13) and Fe2Cl2(m-dobdc) (Table S18), respectively. In addition, the XPS spectra of both materials, while not quantitative,[69] revealed weaker-than-expected signals for Cl in the high-resolution spectra (Figures S98 and S125). Last, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) of both materials revealed relatively uniform distributions of Fe and O species among particles, but more sparse Cl occupancies on the particle surfaces (SI Figures S104 and S131). Together, these results indicate that the charge-balancing anions are likely a mixture of Cl− and OH− in both Fe2X2(dobdc) and Fe2X2(m-dobdc) (X = Cl, OH).

It is well-known that MOFs containing Fe-based secondary building units demonstrate higher electrical conductivities compared to frameworks constructed from other first row transition metals, which makes them promising materials for applications such as chemiresistive sensing and electrocatalysis.[70,71] Notably, Fe2X2(dobdc) and Fe2X2(m-dobdc) (X = Cl, OH) were found to possess pressed-pellet conductivities on the order of 10−7 S/cm (SI Figure S132, SI Table S20), approximately one order of magnitude higher than the electrical conductivity reported for Fe2(dobdc).[71] In particular, Fe2X2(dobdc) (X = Cl, OH) demonstrates a pressed-pellet conductivity of 6.6 × 10−7 S/cm, which is similar to the reported value of 5.8 × 10−7 S/cm for Fe2(dsbdc) (dsbdc4− = 2,5-sulfidobenzene-1,4-dicarboxylate), the previously reported record pressed-pellet conductivity for a MOF-74 analogue.[70] In addition, compared to the known Fe(II) MOFs, the Fe(III) MOFs reported herein offer a significant improvement in their air and moisture stability, as both can be synthesized and washed in air while retaining their crystallinity.[63] Overall, the successful syntheses of Fe2X2(m-dobdc) and Fe2X2(dobdc) (X = Cl, OH) under only ionothermal conditions demonstrate that ionothermal methods can provide access to new and robust MOFs with improved properties.

## Conclusion

Ionothermal synthesis of MOFs offers a benchtop-scalable alternative to traditional syntheses under dilute solvothermal conditions. In addition, the simple ionothermal conditions reported herein eschew the need for complex instrumentation required for mechanochemical methods, maximizing their user-friendliness for non-experts interested in synthesizing MOFs. Additionally, we report purification methods that are optimized for simplicity (soaking in solvents) and for minimizing the amount of organic solvents required (via Soxhlet extraction), resulting in MOFs with comparable surface areas to those washed using larger solvent volumes. In particular, DMF could be completely avoided during the synthesis of six out of nine of the frameworks prepared herein. This unique approach to ionothermal synthesis involves the metal (hydrate) salt playing two roles: as the MOF precursor and as the reaction solvent. Employing this ionothermal method, we report the synthesis of seven known azolate and salicylate MOFs with high crystallinities and BET surface areas comparable to materials synthesized under traditional conditions. Additionally, we report the synthesis and pressed-pellet conductivities of two new M(III) salicylate MOFs. These frameworks represent the first directly synthesized Fe(III) MOF-74 analogues and possess improved air stabilities compared to their Fe(II) analogues. Future work will focus on strategies to reduce ionothermal synthesis temperatures to minimize graphitization, designing new low-melting metal precursors to further generalize this strategy to the preparation of other metal-organic materials, and modification of the ionothermal conditions to improve yields.
